questions.stem: How does Sunset Boulevard begin?
options: With Norma Desmond being filmed at the height of her silent career
With Betty Schaefer rejecting one of Joe's stories at Paramount
With police finding a man's body floating in a mansion's swimming pool
With Joe Gillis arriving in Hollywood from Ohio to look for work
questions.explanation: The film opens with police cars racing along Sunset Boulevard and a body in Norma Desmond's pool. The rest of the film is a flashback explaining how the man, Joe Gillis, came to be there.

questions.stem: Why does Joe Gillis first turn into the driveway of Norma Desmond's mansion?
options: He has been sent by Paramount to collect Norma's old car for a film
He is looking for Max, who has written to him about a job as a writer
He is escaping men sent to repossess his car and gets a flat tyre
He has been invited to discuss a screenplay that Norma wants written
questions.explanation: Joe is broke and behind on his car payments. Fleeing the repossession men, he blows a tyre and pulls into what looks like an abandoned driveway, which is how chance and debt bring him to Norma.

questions.stem: When Joe arrives, Norma mistakes him for:
options: an undertaker who has come to bury her pet chimpanzee
a newspaper reporter who has come to write about her career
a studio messenger bringing her an offer to make a new film
a debt collector sent to take away her furniture and car
questions.explanation: Norma's chimpanzee has died and she is expecting the undertaker. The night-time funeral of the chimp is an early sign of how strange and isolated her world has become.

questions.stem: What job does Norma give Joe?
options: Editing her screenplay for Salome, the film she plans as her comeback
Writing letters to her fans in reply to the mail she receives each day
Driving her car to Paramount for meetings with Cecil B. DeMille
Teaching her how to speak on screen now that films have sound
questions.explanation: Norma has written an enormous script for Salome, in which she will star. Joe, desperate for money, agrees to edit it, and he soon moves into the house.

questions.stem: What happens on New Year's Eve?
options: Joe proposes to Betty at Artie's party, and Norma hears of it from Max
Norma learns that Paramount only wants her car, and refuses to leave her room
Max tells Joe that he was Norma's first husband and her first director
Joe leaves Norma's party for Artie's, then returns after she cuts her wrists
questions.explanation: Norma throws a party for just the two of them. Joe walks out to a friend's party, where he phones Max and learns Norma has slashed her wrists. He goes back, and from then on is more deeply trapped.

questions.stem: Why do Paramount keep phoning Norma's house?
options: They want her to give up the house so it can be used as a set
They want to hire her vintage car for a film, not to make Salome
They want her to play a small part as herself in a DeMille epic
They want to buy the rights to her Salome script for another star
questions.explanation: Norma believes the calls mean the studio wants her comeback. In fact an assistant wants to rent her old Isotta-Fraschini car. Max and DeMille keep the truth from her, protecting her illusion.

questions.stem: How does Norma learn about Joe's relationship with Betty?
options: Artie tells Norma at the New Year's Eve party that Joe loves Betty
She finds the script he is writing with Betty and phones Betty about him
Max follows Joe to Paramount at night and reports what he sees
Betty comes to the house to ask Norma to let Joe go back to writing
questions.explanation: Norma discovers the screenplay with Betty's name on it and rings Betty to hint at the kind of man Joe is. Joe takes the phone and invites Betty to see for herself.

questions.stem: Why does Joe tell Betty he is happy living with Norma, and send her away?
options: He has fallen in love with Norma and no longer wants to write with Betty
Max has warned him that Norma will harm herself again if Betty stays
He believes Betty deserves better than him and wants to free her from him
Norma has threatened to report Betty to Paramount unless he sends her away
questions.explanation: Joe acts the cynical kept man so that Betty will leave him and marry Artie. It is the one selfless act of a character who has mostly given in, and it comes just before he finally tries to leave.

questions.stem: How does Joe die?
options: Max shoots him to stop him from telling Norma the truth about her fans
He drowns in the pool after drinking at Norma's New Year's Eve party
Norma poisons him when she learns that he plans to go back to Ohio
Norma shoots him as he walks out of the house, and he falls into the pool
questions.explanation: When Joe packs to go home to Ohio, Norma shoots him in the back and he falls into the pool, the image the film opened with. The flashback has caught up with the beginning.

questions.stem: What does Norma believe is happening when she walks down the staircase at the end?
options: She is filming a scene from Salome for Cecil B. DeMille
She is being arrested and taken away to answer for the shooting
She is attending the premiere of her comeback film at Paramount
She is greeting her fans at the gates of her house on Sunset Boulevard
questions.explanation: The newsreel cameras have come to film the arrest, and Max directs her as if on set. Norma, now completely lost in her fantasy, plays Salome and moves toward the camera for her close-up.

questions.stem: Who is Max von Mayerling, Norma's butler, revealed to be?
options: Her first husband and the director who discovered her and made her a star
A former film critic who once wrote the reviews that ended her career
Her former leading man, who now works for her because he lost his money
Paramount's old head of publicity, who was sent to watch over her
questions.explanation: Max was a great director who discovered Norma, married her and now serves her. His devotion keeps her illusion alive: he even writes her fan letters, so his love is also part of her ruin.

questions.stem: Who secretly writes the fan letters that Norma receives?
options: Joe, so that she will stay in a good mood while he edits her script
Betty, so that Norma will think Paramount's readers admire her work
DeMille, out of kindness for a star he directed in the silent era
Max, so that she will keep believing she is still loved by the public
questions.explanation: Max invents the letters to protect Norma from the truth that her audience has forgotten her. It shows how carefully her fantasy is built and kept up by others.

questions.stem: Betty Schaefer is best described as:
options: Norma's lawyer, who manages her money and her many old contracts
a studio executive who wants to make Norma's Salome with a new star
a young Paramount script reader who sees real talent in Joe's writing
a former silent star who warns Joe about what Hollywood did to Norma
questions.explanation: Betty first criticises one of Joe's stories, then encourages him to develop a better idea. She stands for honest work, youth and the future, the opposite of the world inside Norma's house.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Joe Gillis at the start of the film?
options: A successful studio writer who is tired of writing Hollywood films
A wealthy fan of silent films who wants to meet his favourite star
A cynical, struggling screenwriter who will compromise to get money
A naive young actor who dreams of becoming a famous movie star
questions.explanation: Joe is broke, his scripts are not selling and he is sceptical of Hollywood. That desperation is why he accepts Norma's money, clothes and comforts, and why he becomes a kept man.

questions.stem: How does the film complicate any simple view of Norma as a villain?
options: It suggests that Joe tricked her into paying for a script he never meant to finish
It shows her as a victim of an industry that made her famous and then discarded her
It reveals in the final scene that Max, not Norma, fired the shots that killed Joe
It shows that she knows her fans have forgotten her but pretends for Max's sake
questions.explanation: Norma is vain, controlling and finally violent, but the film also shows her loneliness, her pride in what silent cinema achieved and how Hollywood used her up. Audiences are invited to pity her as well as judge her.

questions.stem: Joe's relationship with Norma reverses the usual gender roles of 1950s films mainly because:
options: she writes the screenplays while he stays at home and keeps the house in order
she is the one who works at Paramount every day while he waits for her calls
she proposes marriage to him, and he accepts only because Max insists on it
she is older and wealthy, and pays for him, while he is financially dependent
questions.explanation: Norma buys Joe's clothes, pays his debts and gives him a gold cigarette case. Joe becomes the 'kept' partner, a reversal that makes his loss of independence and self-respect clear.

questions.stem: What change in the film industry left stars like Norma Desmond behind?
options: The move from silent films to films with sound in the late 1920s
The move from black-and-white films to colour films in the 1960s
The rise of television, which closed most cinemas by the 1930s
The shift of film production from Hollywood to New York studios
questions.explanation: 'Talkies' arrived in the late 1920s. Stars whose acting relied on faces and gesture, and whose voices didn't suit sound, often lost their careers. Norma blames sound for shrinking the art she loved.

questions.stem: Why is it significant that Norma is played by Gloria Swanson?
options: Swanson had written the screenplay, so the story was based on her own life
Swanson was a famous singer, so the film could add musical numbers for her
Swanson was a real silent-era star, which blurs the line between actor and role
Swanson was a new actress, so audiences had no image of her from other films
questions.explanation: Like Norma, Swanson had been one of the biggest stars of silent film. The film Norma watches at home is a real Swanson silent, Queen Kelly, directed by Erich von Stroheim, who plays Max.

questions.stem: Real silent-film figures, including Buster Keaton, appear as Norma's card-playing friends. Joe calls them 'the waxworks'. What does this suggest?
options: That Joe admires Norma's friends and wants to be accepted by them
That Hollywood has turned its former stars into relics, frozen in the past
That Norma's friends are secretly working for Paramount to watch her
That silent stars were more talented than the actors of the 1950s
questions.explanation: 'Waxworks' makes the guests seem lifeless, like figures in a museum. Casting real forgotten stars sharpens the film's criticism of an industry that discards people once they stop earning money.

questions.stem: Why does Cecil B. DeMille playing himself at Paramount matter to the film?
options: It shows that DeMille plans to cast Norma as the lead in his next picture
It proves that Paramount owns the rights to Norma's Salome screenplay
It reveals that DeMille was the director who first discovered Norma
It sets Norma's fantasy against the real, working Hollywood that has moved on
questions.explanation: DeMille is shown busy on a real production, kind to Norma but unwilling to tell her the truth. The real studio, real director and real film make the gap between Norma's dream and Hollywood as it is hard to miss.

questions.stem: Sunset Boulevard is often discussed as a film noir. Which feature of the film best fits that genre?
options: Wide outdoor landscapes and a lone hero on horseback
A cynical narrator, a crime and dark, shadowy lighting
Song-and-dance numbers performed on elaborate stage sets
A cheerful romance that ends with a wedding and a kiss
questions.explanation: Film noir uses world-weary voiceover, moral corruption, death and low-key lighting with deep shadows. Sunset Boulevard uses these conventions but sets them in Hollywood itself.

questions.stem: Which theme is most central to Sunset Boulevard?
options: The gap between illusion and reality, especially in Hollywood
The rewards of hard work and honesty in a fair industry
The importance of family loyalty across generations
The danger of technology replacing human workers
questions.explanation: Norma lives inside a fantasy of her own stardom, kept up by Max, and Hollywood itself sells dreams. The film keeps exposing the reality behind the image, until Norma loses touch with reality completely.

questions.stem: How does the film present fame?
options: As something fragile, which the industry gives and then takes away
As a fair reward that lasts as long as an actor keeps working hard
As a burden that stars are glad to be free of when they retire
As unimportant to Norma, who cares only for her art and not her image
questions.explanation: Norma was once adored by millions and is now forgotten. Her desperate wish to be loved again shows how fame can define a person and leave them with nothing when it goes.

questions.stem: How does the film explore compromise and selling out?
options: Betty gives up her own writing to become an actress at Norma's suggestion
Max refuses all payment from Norma because he values his art above money
Norma agrees to sell Salome to Paramount so that a younger star can play it
Joe trades his integrity as a writer for comfort and money in Norma's house
questions.explanation: Joe accepts Norma's money, clothes and pool, and gives up his own writing. Working with Betty at night is his attempt to recover something honest, which is why the film makes his choice between the two so important.

questions.stem: What does the film suggest about the way Hollywood treats ageing, particularly for women?
options: That an industry that values youth and beauty leaves older actresses with no place
That older actresses are given the best roles because of their long experience
That ageing matters only to Norma, while the industry welcomes older stars
That actors and actresses are treated equally as they grow older in the industry
questions.explanation: Norma's beauty treatments and her refusal to accept her age come from an industry that judged women on their looks. Joe's line that being fifty is only tragic if you try to be twenty-five puts this bluntly.

questions.stem: What is unusual about the film's voiceover narration?
options: It is spoken by Joe, the dead man whose body is found at the start
It is spoken by Norma, looking back on her career from old age
It is spoken by a police officer reading his report of the crime
It is spoken by Max, who reveals his secrets at the end of the film
questions.explanation: Joe narrates his own story after his death. His dry, cynical tone shapes how the audience sees Norma and Hollywood, and the dead narrator gives the film its dark irony.

questions.stem: What is the effect of telling most of the story as a flashback?
options: The audience learns what happens to Norma after she is arrested
The audience knows Joe dies, so they watch for how and why it happens
The audience is surprised by Joe's death when it comes in the last scene
The audience can see events from Norma's point of view, not Joe's
questions.explanation: Because the ending is shown first, suspense comes from how events lead to the pool, not whether they will. Joe's decisions feel doomed, which suits the film's noir mood.

questions.stem: The opening shot shows Joe's body from below the water, looking up at the police. What does this suggest?
options: That the film will be a light comedy about life in Hollywood
That the story will be seen from the dead man's point of view
That the police are the main characters whose story will follow
That the pool is the most expensive feature of Norma's house
questions.explanation: Looking up from beneath Joe places the camera with the dead man, who narrates. It is a striking, disturbing image that announces the story's darkness from the first minutes.

questions.stem: How does the mise-en-scène of Norma's house reflect her character?
options: It is crowded with scripts, showing how hard she works at her craft
It is grand but decaying and filled with photographs of her younger self
It is modern and bright, showing that she has embraced the new Hollywood
It is small and bare, showing that she has given up on wealth and fame
questions.explanation: The mansion is huge, old-fashioned and neglected, and dozens of images of young Norma fill the rooms. The setting shows a woman living in the past and surrounded by her own legend.

questions.stem: In the final shot, Norma moves toward the camera and the image blurs. What is the effect?
options: It shows Joe's spirit leaving the house as his narration comes to an end
It shows Norma escaping from the police into the garden in the darkness
It shows her slipping completely into her fantasy as reality dissolves
It shows that the newsreel camera has broken during the arrest scene
questions.explanation: Norma looks straight into the lens, as if into her audience, and the image goes out of focus. The blurring of the picture mirrors her total loss of the line between film and life.

questions.stem: Joe compares Norma to Miss Havisham from Great Expectations, who wore her rotting wedding dress for decades after being jilted. What does the allusion suggest?
options: Norma plans to marry Joe and is preparing for an expensive wedding
Norma is a cruel guardian who raises Joe to hurt other people
Norma is secretly poor and has been hiding her debts from Max
Norma has frozen her life at the moment her fame was taken from her
questions.explanation: Miss Havisham never moved on from being jilted, keeping her wedding dress and veil as they were. The comparison suggests Norma, too, lives in a preserved past, refusing to let time move on since Hollywood left her behind.

questions.stem: Who says 'I am big. It's the pictures that got small.'?
options: Max, defending Norma to the police at the end of the film
DeMille, speaking to Norma on the set of his new picture
Joe, mocking the films that Paramount makes in the 1950s
Norma, answering Joe's remark that she used to be big
questions.explanation: When Joe recognises her as someone who 'used to be big', Norma insists that she is still a great star and that the films themselves have shrunk. It shows her pride and her refusal to accept change.

questions.stem: What does Norma's line 'We didn't need dialogue. We had faces!' reveal?
options: Her view that Joe's dialogue is the best part of her screenplay
Her belief that silent film was a purer art than the talkies
Her fear that she cannot remember the lines in her own script
Her wish to write a film that has no characters or story at all
questions.explanation: Norma believes silent actors told stories through expression and that sound has cheapened cinema. The line is part self-defence, but it also carries a real argument about what was lost.

questions.stem: When Norma says 'All right, Mr. DeMille, I'm ready for my close-up', what is the irony?
options: Norma knows she is being arrested and is joking with the police
The close-up she asks for was cut from the film by Paramount
The cameras are newsreel cameras filming her arrest, not a film set
DeMille is standing beside her, ready to begin filming Salome at last
questions.explanation: Norma believes she is making her comeback, but the cameras are recording her arrest for murder. The famous line marks her final escape into fantasy.

questions.stem: Joe's voiceover says, 'Funny how gentle people get with you once you're dead.' What does it show about his narration?
options: Its dark, dry humour, even about his own death
Its anger at Norma for shooting him in the back
Its sadness at leaving Betty behind for good
Its fear of what will happen to Max and Norma
questions.explanation: As the police lift his body from the pool, Joe comments on it with detached, ironic wit. The cynical humour is typical of his narration and of film noir.

questions.stem: Joe tells Norma, 'There's nothing tragic about being fifty. Not unless you try to be twenty-five.' What idea does this express?
options: That Norma's suffering comes from refusing to accept her age
That Norma is too young to give up hope of a comeback in films
That Joe believes age makes no difference in the film industry
That being fifty is the most tragic age for a Hollywood actress
questions.explanation: Joe says this as he finally leaves, puncturing her illusion. The tragedy, he argues, is not age itself but her denial of it, though the film also shows Hollywood encouraged that denial.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Sunset Boulevard shows Hollywood as a place that destroys the people who serve it.' Discuss.
options: In Sunset Boulevard, Norma Desmond is a former star of silent films who lives on Sunset Boulevard
This essay will discuss how Hollywood is shown in the film Sunset Boulevard by Billy Wilder
Sunset Boulevard is a famous film made by Billy Wilder in 1950 for the Paramount studio
Wilder suggests that Hollywood uses people for profit and abandons them when they stop earning
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without making an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Norma lives in a huge mansion with lots of photos of herself.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Add the address of the mansion and the year in which it was supposedly built
List more objects that are found inside the mansion, such as the organ
Describe what happens in the mansion later in the film, scene by scene
Explain how the photographs show Norma clinging to an image of her younger self
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Saying the photographs show Norma worshipping her past self links the detail to the film's ideas about illusion and fame.
